name: Fasting-mimicking diet
lead: The fasting-mimicking diet (FMD) is a five-day, low-calorie, low-protein, plant-based eating cycle designed to reproduce some physiological effects of water fasting while still supplying limited food. It was developed by biogerontologist Valter Longo at the University of Southern California.[1]

Per Grokipedia, a typical cycle supplies roughly 1,000 kcal on day one and about 700 to 800 kcal on days two to five, repeated every one to six months; a commercial version, ProLon, is sold by L-Nutra, founded in 2009.[1]

Its main research focus is aging, metabolic and disease markers rather than appearance, though it is discussed in looksmaxxing circles for fat loss and skin or "longevity" aims. Human data come from a randomized trial of 100 healthy participants and studies in cancer patients; much other work is in mice.[2][3][4]
infobox: Low calorie, low protein, plant-based, higher unsaturated fat

paras: Unlike intermittent fasting patterns such as time-restricted eating, the FMD is a short periodic cycle rather than a daily or weekly routine. Its nutrient composition is low in calories, sugars and protein and high in unsaturated fats, intended to trigger fasting-like responses.[1][2]

Longo's group at USC studied fasting and nutrient-sensing pathways from the early 2000s, and the FMD was formalised in the mid-2010s, with a 2015 paper in Cell Metabolism describing a periodic diet that mimics fasting in mice.[1] L-Nutra was founded in 2009 to commercialise the approach.[1]

A 2017 randomized trial in 100 generally healthy US participants tested repeated FMD cycles against a control diet on markers and risk factors associated with aging, diabetes, cancer and cardiovascular disease.[2]
A 2022 study in cancer patients reported the diet to be safe in that setting and examined effects on metabolism and antitumor immunity.[3]
The multicentre randomized phase 2 DIRECT trial examined the FMD as an adjunct to neoadjuvant chemotherapy in breast cancer.[4]
No studies were found measuring effects on facial appearance, skin or body composition as primary appearance outcomes.

Mouse studies have examined the FMD in models of multiple sclerosis, cancer immunity, breast cancer with hormone therapy, diabetes with beta-cell regeneration, inflammatory bowel disease and Parkinson disease.[5][6][7][8][9][10]
Grokipedia notes it is not intended as a daily diet and should be undertaken under medical supervision, particularly with eating disorders, pregnancy or certain medical conditions.[1]

timeline.event: L-Nutra founded to commercialise the diet.[1]
Longo and colleagues publish the periodic diet in mice in Cell Metabolism.[1]
Randomized trial in 100 healthy participants published in Science Translational Medicine.[2]
DIRECT trial in breast cancer published.[4]

card.summary: A five-day low-calorie cycle from Valter Longo; studied for aging markers and disease, not for looks.
card.note: Human appearance outcomes untested; supervision advised in pregnancy or eating disorders.

quick.overview:
The fasting-mimicking diet is a five-day plant-based, low-calorie, low-protein cycle created by Valter Longo, repeated every few months.

Human trials examine aging and disease markers and cancer-care settings; no study has tested appearance outcomes.
quick.mechanism: It aims to trigger fasting-like responses, such as lower IGF-1 and increased autophagy, without total food abstinence.
quick.risks: Intended as periodic, not daily. Medical supervision is advised with eating disorders, pregnancy or medical conditions.
